newsitem.title: FIJI: FEATURE-South Pacific cruising is missing the boat.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-South Pacific cruising is missing the boat.

text.p: Cruise ships full to the gunwales with ladies and gentlemen in their finery once docked in this South Pacific port, disgorging such notable passengers as American writer Mark Twain.
The waterfront Grand Pacific Hotel was built in the early 1900s by the Union Steamship Company with an interior that replicated the inside of a cruise ship to make passengers feel at home.

Today, cruise ships are few and far between and the Grand Pacific Hotel is boarded up, its only guests pigeons and water rats. The Pacific Ocean still boasts a small cruise industry, but ships now drop anchor elsewhere.
The world cruise industry is booming, but the palm-fringed islands of the South Pacific are missing the boat.
The region's main cruise operator, P&O Australia Holidays, says Australia and the South Pacific is an expensive and over-regulated cruise region, which risks being marginalised.

The firm's managing director, Phil Young, says the region has an opportunity to become a major cruise centre both because of the 2000 Sydney Olympics and because it is on the doorstep of Asia, which is witnessing a rapid expansion in cruising.
"Once-in-a-lifetime opportunities. Yet, at the moment we are not in a position to take advantage of them," Young said.
"In fact, we are facing a situation where, if we do not move quickly we are in danger of missing the boat altogether."
The world cruise industry is worth an estimated US$15 billion a year, but the Australia-South Pacific slice is only A$200 million ($158 million), according to cruise operators.
In 1994, more than four million people took a cruise; for 1996 the figure is forecast to reach six million; and by the year 2000 eight million are expected to holiday on board a ship.

"International growth in the last 10 years has been driven by the American market," Young told Reuters in Sydney. "The American middle class has woken up to the magic of a cruise holiday. Many work in the Midwest and rarely see the sea."
Cruise operators are currently building 29 new ships, worth US$9.0 billion, destined primarily for the world's major cruise region, the Caribbean, over the next three years, says Young.
This influx of new ships will leave operators looking for a new region for their older ships, offering Australia and the South Pacific another unique opportunity for growth, says Young.

But Australia's cabotage laws make it prohibitively expensive to base a foreign ship in Australia, the hub of South Pacific cruising. Its six states charge individual port fees and ships face myriad charges including one for using port lights.
P&O's 39-year-old Fairstar and two CTC Cruise Line ships, are the only ships operating out of Sydney on a regular basis.

"While the restrictions contained in this outdated regulation exist, Australia is not going to be very attractive to overseas operators and it will continue to be difficult to develop exclusively Australian itineraries," says Young.

A burgeoning Asian middle class has in the past few years also discovered the pleasures of a sea voyage. But Asians prefer shorter cruises to Americans -- just out to sea and back, as long as the ship has a casino.

Australian cruise ships are unable to open casinos or duty free shops unless they travel to a foreign port, a minimum of two or three days sailing, which, Young says, is a major disincentive to coastal cruising and a barrier to picking up Asian gamblers already visiting casinos on the Australian coast.
Asia is experiencing staggering growth in cruising.

In 1991 Singapore's cruise industry was in its infancy. Today it boasts a million passengers a year, one sixth of the world market. Malaysia posted 256,000 passengers in 1994, compared with 14,700 two years earlier.
Asian governments have also cut the bureaucratic regulations governing cruise ships, thus saving operators millions and making their destinations more attractive.

In contrast, P&O spends around US$280,000 a year on ship manifests because of a requirement to fly immigration officers to Pacific islands to inspect passenger passports -- a hangover from a bygone cruising era before computers and fax machines fascimiles.
Cruise operators say Australia and the South Pacific could easily increase their share of the world market if some of the bureaucratic regulations were eased.
Then the rats and pigeons could be evicted from Fiji's Grand Pacific Hotel and its elegant cabins could once again play host to shiploads of holidaymakers.
